data.prompt: Which of these is made of atoms?

options.label: The light from a lamp
options.note: Light is energy, not matter.

options.label: A shadow
options.note: A shadow is just a place where light is blocked.

options.label: A sound
options.note: Sound is a wave moving through matter; it is not matter itself.

data.explanation: A grain of salt is matter, so it is made of atoms. Light, shadows and sounds are not matter.

data.prompt: Everything you can touch is made of ___.
data.explanation: Everything you can touch is made of atoms.

data.prompt: Put these in order from smallest to largest.

items.label: The width of a human hair

data.explanation: An atom is far smaller than even a single cell. A red blood cell is a few thousandths of a millimetre across, a hair is about 0.07 mm wide and a grain of rice is a few millimetres long.

data.prompt: Which of these are made of atoms? Sort each one.
data.explanation: Phones and apples are matter, and matter is made of atoms. Light and heat are forms of energy, not matter.

data.statement: Atoms are too small to be seen with an ordinary light microscope.
data.explanation: True. An ordinary microscope uses visible light, whose waves are far longer than an atom is wide. Special instruments can image atoms, but a classroom microscope cannot.

data.prompt: Where is almost all of an atom's mass?

options.label: In the electrons
options.note: Electrons are incredibly light: a proton is about 1,800 times heavier.

options.label: Spread evenly through the atom
options.note: The mass is not spread out: it is packed into the nucleus.

options.label: An atom has hardly any mass
options.note: Atoms are tiny, but they do have mass, and nearly all of it is in the nucleus.

data.explanation: The nucleus holds almost all of the mass. A proton or neutron is about 1,800 times heavier than an electron.

data.prompt: Tap the nucleus of the atom.
data.explanation: The nucleus is the tiny centre of the atom. Protons and neutrons live there. The electrons are outside it.

data.prompt: Match each particle to its charge.
data.explanation: Protons are positive, neutrons have no charge and electrons are negative.

data.prompt: Imagine an atom blown up to the size of a football stadium. How big would its nucleus be?
data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The reveal comes later in the lesson.

data.prompt: Where is each particle? Sort them.
data.explanation: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus. Electrons are outside it.

data.statement: The nucleus takes up most of the space in an atom.
data.explanation: Myth. The nucleus is a tiny speck at the centre. Nearly all of the atom's size is the region where its electrons are found.

data.prompt: What makes an atom of gold different from an atom of oxygen?

options.label: They have different numbers of protons
They are made of different kinds of stuff
options.note: Every atom is built from the same three particles. Only the numbers differ.

options.label: Gold atoms are solid and oxygen atoms are hollow
options.note: Atoms of every element are mostly empty space around a tiny nucleus.

options.label: Gold atoms are yellow
options.note: Single atoms do not have a colour in this sense. The difference is the proton count.

data.explanation: Gold atoms have 79 protons and oxygen atoms have 8. The particles are the same kinds; the number of protons is what differs.

data.prompt: An atom with 6 protons is always ___.
data.explanation: Carbon is the element with 6 protons. Its atomic number is 6.

data.prompt: Tap element number 8.
data.explanation: Element 8 is oxygen (symbol O). Its atomic number is 8, so every oxygen atom has 8 protons.

data.prompt: Match each symbol to its element.
data.explanation: Symbols are short names for elements, usually the first one or two letters of the name: C for carbon, O for oxygen, H for hydrogen and He for helium.

data.prompt: Put these elements in order of atomic number, lowest first.
data.explanation: Hydrogen is 1, carbon is 6 and oxygen is 8. The periodic table lists the elements in this order.

data.prompt: What is the real difference between an atom of gold and an atom of oxygen?

options.label: They have different numbers of protons
They are made of different kinds of stuff
Gold atoms are solid balls and oxygen atoms are hollow

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. Find out as you build.

data.statement: If you changed the number of protons in an atom, it would become a different element.
data.explanation: True. The number of protons is the atomic number, and it alone decides which element an atom is.

data.prompt: What do isotopes of the same element share?

options.label: The same number of neutrons
options.note: Different neutron counts are exactly what makes them different isotopes.

options.label: The same mass
options.note: Different neutron counts give different masses.

options.label: Nothing: they are different elements
options.note: Isotopes of one element are the same element. They share their proton count.

data.explanation: Isotopes of an element all have the same number of protons, which is why they are the same element. They differ in neutrons.

data.prompt: A carbon atom with 6 protons and 7 neutrons is called carbon-___.
data.explanation: Add the protons and neutrons: 6 + 7 = 13. So this is carbon-13.

data.prompt: Carbon-14 has 6 protons and ___ neutrons.
data.explanation: The 14 is the mass number: protons plus neutrons. Carbon has 6 protons, so 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons.

data.prompt: Match each carbon atom to its name. The number in the name is protons plus neutrons.
Two atoms are both carbon. Can one be heavier than the other?

options.label: Yes, they can have different masses
No, all carbon atoms are identical

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. Build a heavier carbon atom in the next card.

data.prompt: Carbon always has 6 protons. Which of these atoms are carbon? Sort each one.
data.explanation: Only the number of protons matters for the element. Any atom with 6 protons is carbon, whatever its neutrons. Those carbon atoms are isotopes of carbon.
Myth. Isotope just means a version of an element with a certain number of neutrons. Most of the atoms around you, including carbon-12, are stable isotopes. Only some isotopes are radioactive.

data.prompt: Which force pushes the protons in a nucleus apart?

options.label: Strong force
options.note: The strong force pulls particles together, not apart.

options.label: Gravity
options.note: Gravity is far too weak to matter between particles this small.

data.explanation: Positive charges push each other apart. The strong force pulls neighbouring particles together and, over the tiny distances inside a nucleus, it wins when the nucleus is stable.

data.prompt: What does an unstable nucleus do over time?

options.label: It changes into a more stable nucleus and gives off radiation
It slowly grows heavier
options.note: Unstable nuclei change by giving something off, they do not keep growing.

options.label: Nothing: unstable just means rare
options.note: Unstable means the nucleus will eventually change.

options.label: It disappears completely
options.note: The nucleus changes into a different nucleus. Nothing vanishes.

data.explanation: An unstable nucleus eventually changes into a more stable one and gives off radiation. That process is radioactivity.

data.prompt: Match each to its effect in the nucleus.
data.explanation: Protons push each other apart. The strong force holds particles together over very short distances. Neutrons feel the strong force but have no charge, so they add glue without adding push.

data.prompt: Protons all carry positive charge, and like charges push apart. So why doesn't the nucleus fly apart?

options.label: Another, stronger force holds the particles together
Nuclei do fly apart all the time

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The next card shows what holds a nucleus together.

data.prompt: Which of these atoms are stable? Sort each one.
data.explanation: Carbon-12 and oxygen-16 are stable. Carbon-14 and uranium-238 are unstable, which means radioactive.

data.statement: Most of the atoms in your body are stable.
data.explanation: True. Almost all of your atoms are stable isotopes of hydrogen, oxygen, carbon and nitrogen. A tiny number are naturally unstable, such as potassium-40.

data.statement: Unstable atoms only exist where humans have made them.
data.explanation: Myth. Unstable atoms occur in nature. Potassium-40 is in bananas and in your own body, and carbon-14 is made in the upper atmosphere.

data.prompt: Roughly how wide is a single atom?

options.label: A few tenths of a nanometre
A few tenths of a micrometre
options.note: That is about the size of a bacterium, thousands of atoms across.

options.label: A few tenths of a millimetre
options.note: That is about the width of a hair, hundreds of thousands of atoms across.

options.label: A few tenths of a metre
options.note: That is about the size of a loaf of bread.

data.explanation: An atom is about a few tenths of a nanometre across: a nanometre is a billionth of a metre.

data.prompt: On the periodic table, what is the whole number in the corner of an element's box?

options.label: The atomic number, which is the number of protons
Number of neutrons
options.note: The corner number counts protons, not neutrons.

options.label: Year of discovery
options.note: That is not shown on the table.

data.explanation: The number in the corner is the atomic number: how many protons each atom of that element has.

data.statement: The electrons of an atom are packed inside the nucleus.
data.explanation: Myth. The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons. Electrons are found outside it, in a region far larger than the nucleus.

data.prompt: Tap carbon (symbol C).
data.explanation: Carbon is element 6, with the symbol C.

data.prompt: About how many atoms would fit side by side across the width of one human hair?

options.label: A few hundred
options.note: That is far too few. Atoms are much smaller than that.

options.label: A few thousand
options.note: Still too few: a hair is far wider than a few thousand atoms.

options.label: A few billion
options.note: That is too many. A hair is wide, but not that wide.

data.explanation: A hair is about 0.07 mm wide and an atom a few tenths of a nanometre, so a few hundred thousand atoms fit across it.

data.statement: Isotopes of one element have different numbers of neutrons.
data.explanation: True. That is what makes them different isotopes of the same element.

data.prompt: What are carbon-12 and carbon-14?

options.label: Two different elements
options.note: Both have 6 protons, so both are carbon.

options.label: Ions of carbon
options.note: Ions differ in electrons. These differ in neutrons.

data.explanation: They are isotopes of carbon: the same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons.

data.prompt: Which particle has a negative electric charge?

options.label: The proton
options.note: Protons are positive.

options.label: The neutron
options.note: Neutrons have no charge.

data.explanation: Electrons are negative. Protons are positive and neutrons have no charge.
True. That is why they are called neutrons.

data.prompt: Which of these is NOT made of atoms?

options.label: The wood in a campfire
options.note: Wood is matter, so it is made of atoms.

options.label: The air around the fire
options.note: Air is matter, so it is made of atoms.

options.label: The ash left behind
options.note: Ash is matter, so it is made of atoms.

options.label: The heat you feel from the fire

data.explanation: Heat is energy, not matter, so it is not made of atoms. The wood, the air and the ash are all matter.

data.prompt: Compared with the whole atom, how big is the nucleus?

options.label: Tiny: a speck at the centre
About half the width of the atom
options.note: The nucleus is vastly smaller than that.

options.label: About the same size as the atom
options.note: The atom is many thousands of times wider than its nucleus.

data.explanation: The nucleus is a tiny speck. The atom is roughly a hundred thousand times wider.

data.prompt: Oxygen-17 has 8 protons and ___ neutrons.
data.explanation: The mass number 17 is protons plus neutrons. 17 - 8 = 9 neutrons.

data.prompt: How many protons does every oxygen atom have?

options.note: Six protons would make it carbon.
16 is oxygen-16's mass number, not its proton count.
Two protons would make it helium.

data.explanation: Oxygen is element 8, so every oxygen atom has 8 protons.

data.statement: Natural potassium, like the potassium in a banana, includes a small amount of a radioactive isotope.
data.explanation: True. Roughly 1 in every 10,000 potassium atoms is potassium-40, which is radioactive.

data.statement: Two atoms with different numbers of protons can be the same element.
data.explanation: Myth. The number of protons decides the element. Different proton counts mean different elements.

data.prompt: What does the strong force do in a nucleus?

options.label: Holds neighbouring protons and neutrons together
Pushes protons apart
options.note: That is the electric force between positive charges.

options.label: Spins the electrons
options.note: The strong force acts inside the nucleus, not on electrons.

data.explanation: The strong force pulls neighbouring protons and neutrons together, but only over very short distances.

data.statement: The strong force reaches across long distances, like gravity.
data.explanation: Myth. The strong force only works over a very short range, about the size of a nucleus. Beyond that it drops to almost nothing.

data.prompt: In the name uranium-235, what does 235 tell you?

options.label: The number of protons plus neutrons
The number of protons
options.note: Uranium always has 92 protons. The 235 counts protons and neutrons together.

options.label: The number of neutrons
options.note: 235 is protons plus neutrons. Uranium-235 has 143 neutrons.

data.explanation: The number is the mass number, protons plus neutrons. Uranium has 92 protons, so uranium-235 has 143 neutrons.

data.prompt: Which of these atoms is unstable?

options.label: Carbon-12
options.note: Carbon-12 is stable.

options.label: Hydrogen-1
options.note: Hydrogen-1 is stable.

options.label: Oxygen-16
options.note: Oxygen-16 is stable.

data.explanation: Carbon-14 has too many neutrons for a stable nucleus, so it is radioactive.

data.statement: A glass of water is made of atoms.
data.explanation: True. Water is matter, and all matter is made of atoms (joined together as molecules of water).
